prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, opening a new regime of precision in the measurement of time

statement.case_for: I keep B005 alone, with Katori and Ye, and the first-round exchange has made me more comfortable with it, not less. The chair asks what the lattice adds beyond 2005 and 2012, and I think it can be said in one sentence. The 2005 prize gave us the ruler that counts optical cycles and the 2012 prize gave us control of a single quantum system, whereas the magic-wavelength lattice made it possible to hold thousands of neutral atoms with the motional and light shifts cancelled, so that accuracy and averaging power arrive together. That is a conceptual step, because it removes the trade-off that limited single-ion clocks between a clean system and a short averaging time. It is also the step that took clocks to the 1e-18 level, where gravitational redshift is seen over millimetres and limits on constants and ultralight dark matter become informative. Eight of eight colleagues name the same two people, and the independent reproduction at JILA, RIKEN and Tokyo, PTB, NIST and SYRTE is the kind of clue from nature that I want before I ask who deserves credit. I see no reason to add a second part. A second prize part would need to be as mature and as cleanly attributed as B005, and none of B035, B014 or B015 is.
statement.case_against: My reservations have narrowed but not disappeared. The overlap with 2005 and 2012 is answerable in the citation, but a sceptical reader can still call this an outstanding refinement of an honoured lineage, and I accept that I am partly relying on the colleagues in atomic physics for that judgement. No variation of a constant and no dark-matter signal has been seen, so the physical payoff so far is tighter bounds, and a quiet null result is a weaker story than a new phenomenon. The redefinition of the second is still pending, and I cannot say that waiting would change the science. It could change the timing and the public reading. Finally, Takamoto, Ludlow, Hinkley, Lemonde and Derevianko did decisive work that two names cannot reflect, and I have not been able to verify the Katori 2001-2003 chronology against parallel proposals from the supplied text.

responses.point: Eriksson asks whether the many-atom lattice step is a real conceptual advance over single-ion clocks or mainly a gain in averaging, and says he leans on Lindroth, Kroll and me for that judgement.
responses.response: I would answer that it is both, and the two cannot be separated. Averaging alone would not help if the atoms were shifted by their own motion and by the trapping light, so the conceptual content is the magic wavelength together with Lamb-Dicke confinement, which turns a large ensemble from a source of error into a resource. Without that idea more atoms would just mean more systematics. That is why I regard it as distinct from the 2012 ion work, and why the sentence in the citation should name the lattice and the regime of precision. I also take your earlier point about Car and Parrinello seriously, and I keep B043 out of my alternatives for the method-versus-discovery reason we both see.

responses.point: Lindroth would keep the citation tied narrowly to the lattice clock, since the comb reads out the optical oscillations while the magic-wavelength lattice gives the clock its stability, and she treats the priority chronology as a drafting matter.
responses.response: I agree with the narrow citation and I have dropped any wording about metrology as a field. I would go one step beyond drafting on chronology, though. Drafting handles the scope but it cannot settle whether Katori's proposal precedes or merely parallels other lattice ideas, and a citation that says 'invention' commits us to that. I would ask the outside experts for the original papers before the vote is final. I accept your point that your quantitative agreement between calculated magic wavelengths, blackbody shifts and measurement is a strong sign that this is a result about nature, not only an instrument, and I will use that argument if a colleague calls it engineering.

responses.point: Olsson asks for Katori's 2001-2003 proposal to be checked against the first strontium lattice-clock measurements and Ye's later comparisons, and warns against the 'second, better version' trap.
responses.response: I support putting that check on the verification list, and I would accept it as a condition for my position, not only a precaution. The test of the 'second, better version' charge is whether the lattice clock could have been inferred from the comb and from ion clocks, and I do not think it could, because the magic-wavelength idea is new and its demonstration came from different people. If the primary papers showed that Katori's contribution was a demonstration of someone else's concept, my view of the two names would change, and I would then want the experts to say who held the concept. I do not expect that, but I cannot confirm it from what is in front of us.

responses.point: Pearce asks whether a two-part prize pairing B005 with a single credited name from B035 would be acceptable, and notes that this seems unfair to Karle and Spiering, while keeping IceCube as first alternative.
responses.response: I would not support a one-name subset of IceCube, and I think you are right that it would be unfair, since the credit among Halzen, Karle and Spiering cannot be split by a drafting convenience. A two-part configuration would also exceed three people in total if IceCube came with all three names beside Katori and Ye, so it is excluded by the limit in any case. I therefore keep B035 as an alternative and not a second part. I would still like the experts to clarify the AMANDA, Baikal and DUMAND lineage and the roles inside IceCube, because I think this is the strongest case for a later prize and a good reason not to let B005 crowd it out by default.

responses.point: Johansson warns that widening the citation to metrology would invite the overlap objection, and notes that the ion-clock and neutral-atom lineages are not fully separated in the credited list.
responses.response: I agree on the citation and have kept the wording to the lattice clock and the regime of precision. On your second point I think the separation is better than you fear. Wineland's prize was for control of single quantum systems, and the credited pair did not work on trapped ions but on neutral atoms in a lattice, so the lineages share tools without sharing the key idea. I would not add an ion-clock name, since that would blur the very distinction the citation relies on. I would rather the citation be narrow and the history be acknowledged in the committee's background text.

uncertainties: Whether primary sources confirm that Katori's magic-wavelength proposal has priority over parallel lattice-clock ideas, which I cannot verify from the supplied text.
Whether the committee should wait for the redefinition of the SI second, or accept that 1e-18 performance and independent reproduction already supply the maturity.
Whether a measured variation of a constant or a dark-matter signal is needed before the physics is regarded as decisive, since only tighter bounds exist so far.
Whether the contributions of Takamoto, Ludlow, Hinkley, Lemonde and Derevianko are properly represented by the two names Katori and Ye.
Whether IceCube attribution among Halzen, Karle and Spiering can be settled for a future prize.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict from my profile for B005 or the other shortlisted candidates. My PhD supervisor David Gross and my frequent co-author Thomas Van Riet are not credited on any shortlisted ballot, and I have no known tie to Katori, Ye or the other credited names. As Secretary I would be the one commissioning the outside expert checks on priority and attribution, and I would treat their answers as evidence on the discovery and not as support for a preferred outcome.
